The texel-density claim following Eq. 2 is incorrect as stated: independently normalizing each part to the unit square and then applying equal scales does not ensure consistent texel density across differently sized surface parts. strengths: The paper addresses useful practical objectives: organizing UV charts around meaningful parts and placing seams in less exposed regions. The modular design is understandable, and the inherited parameterization backbone is explicitly credited.

The reported visibility improvement is substantial: Table 1 reduces mean seam exposure from 0.8604 for FlexPara and 0.7855 for OptCuts to 0.6065, while retaining comparable conformality to FlexPara. Qualitative examples support the intended effect.

The 115-participant preference study provides encouraging perceptual evidence. The appendix also includes segmentation alternatives, combined semantic/visibility results, packing experiments, and training-time measurements.
weaknesses: The contribution is incremental and insufficiently isolated. Semantic awareness largely consists of established segmentation followed by an existing parameterizer; the visibility contribution adds a soft AO-weighted seam loss. Crucially, there is no comparison against applying conventional unwrappers to the same semantic partitions. Such a control is needed to establish the neural method's added value. Relevant prior semantic and visibility-aware methods are discussed but not experimentally compared.

Several central claims exceed the algorithm described. Hard segmentation, graph cuts, and discrete packing do not constitute an end-to-end differentiable semantic objective. Independently trained charts and row-major placement provide no explicit matching of part identities, chart orientations, or coordinates across shapes, so cross-shape correspondence and texture-transfer claims remain unsupported. Additionally, uniformly scaling independently normalized islands does not guarantee consistent texel density, contrary to the statement following Eq. 2.

Validity as a triangle-mesh parameterization is insufficiently established. The method predicts one UV coordinate per vertex and detects seams through neighborhood separation, but does not adequately explain vertex duplication, connectivity changes, or treatment of triangles crossing cuts. Cycle consistency and local vertex repulsion do not guarantee triangle-level injectivity. Flip rates, overlap measurements, and surface-coverage checks are absent.

The quantitative evaluation and reproducibility details are incomplete. The aggregate benchmark's mesh count, provenance, preprocessing, and aggregation protocol are unclear. Semantic accuracy uses SAMesh predictions as ground truth, measuring agreement with another algorithm rather than independently validated semantics. Important optimization settings, seam temperatures, hardware, and baseline configurations are missing. The abstract announces public code but supplies no link.

The visibility objective and evaluation leave important ambiguities. Mean seam AO can improve by adding low-exposure seam regions without reducing total exposed seam length; no corresponding length-controlled evaluation is provided. AO also does not directly measure visibility under a specified camera distribution. Meanwhile, equiareality falls from 0.6759 to 0.6093 versus FlexPara and is substantially below OptCuts' 0.8934, contradicting the claim that visibility optimization does not harm geometric quality. A controlled distortion–visibility trade-off analysis is needed.

The preference study does not establish the broader workflow benefits claimed. It covers only 11 comparison items, with no reported uncertainty or randomization protocol. Checkerboard scales and highlighted regions differ across methods in Fig. 9, complicating attribution of preferences specifically to seam placement. No actual texture-generation, cross-shape transfer, or editing-efficiency experiment demonstrates the proposed downstream advantages.

The main runtime comparison obscures the cost of obtaining a parameterization for a new mesh. Table 1 lists 2 seconds for the visibility-aware method against 240 seconds for OptCuts, but Appendix A.3 clarifies that the neural figure excludes per-mesh optimization. Table 9 reports an average optimization cost of 31,160 seconds, approximately 8.7 hours and 24 times FlexPara's cost. End-to-end timings are essential for assessing the claimed practical utility.

strengths: Addresses a practically relevant problem: producing UV charts that support semantic editing while placing seams in less exposed regions.

The visibility objective has encouraging evidence. Table 1 reports mean seam exposure of 0.6065 versus 0.8604 for FlexPara and 0.7855 for OptCuts; qualitative examples and the loss ablation support this improvement.

The 115-participant preference study provides supporting perceptual evidence. The appendix also includes architecture details, alternative partitioners, packing experiments, and training-time measurements.
weaknesses: The methodological contribution is limited and insufficiently isolated. The semantic pipeline combines established segmentation, an explicitly reused parameterization backbone, and grid packing. A crucial baseline is the same segmentation followed by conventional UV parameterization. Comparisons against the cited methods specifically targeting semantic mapping or inconspicuous seams are also missing.

Central claims exceed the implemented mechanism. Equation 1 contains inherited geometric losses rather than a new semantic alignment objective. Independently trained parts and row-major packing do not establish consistent chart locations or orientations across shapes, and cross-shape correspondence or texture transfer is not evaluated. Describing the entire framework as end-to-end differentiable also overlooks discrete segmentation and component relabeling.

UV validity is insufficiently established. Cycle consistency and local vertex repulsion do not guarantee nonoverlapping, consistently oriented triangles. The conversion from pointwise UV predictions to a cut mesh with duplicated seam vertices is insufficiently specified, and overlap or flipped-triangle statistics are absent. Additionally, equal scaling after independently normalizing each chart does not guarantee the consistent texel density claimed in Section 3.3.

The evaluation is difficult to assess and reproduce: mesh sources, evaluation-set sizes, aggregation details, and uncertainty are insufficiently documented. SAMesh predictions are treated as semantic ground truth without independent validation. The user study covers only 11 comparisons and lacks reported randomization and uncertainty analysis. Important optimization and seam-smoothing settings are missing, and the supplied PDF provides no usable implementation link.

Mean seam AO measures essentially the optimized surrogate, rather than total visible seam burden. It can decrease by adding low-exposure seams without removing existing exposed seams. Quantitative controls for seam length and viewpoint-dependent visibility are missing, and the checkerboard examples do not establish benefits for actual texture synthesis, editing, or transfer.

Claims that visibility optimization does not harm geometric quality are inconsistent with the reported trade-off. Equiareality decreases from 0.6759 to 0.6093 in Table 1. For semantic mapping, Table 3 reports both lower conformality and lower equiareality than multi-chart FlexPara. Matched-distortion comparisons or weight sweeps are needed to establish whether the perceptual gains justify these losses.

The main runtime comparisons omit mandatory per-mesh fitting. Table 1 reports a 2-second neural forward pass alongside OptCuts' optimization time, whereas Table 9 reports average visibility-aware training of 31,160 seconds, approximately 8.7 hours and 24 times FlexPara's training time. Although disclosed in the appendix, this substantially weakens practical efficiency and requires end-to-end comparisons.
